rows.title: #1 · Foundational Physics Facts and Extremes
sub: Group-I F18: Science and Technology - Nature and Scope, Relevance to Daily Life, National S&T Policy

x: Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #1, pages 2-4
Newton formulated the first law of motion.
The first nuclear reactor producing a controlled chain reaction was Chicago Pile-1.
Enrico Fermi was associated with Chicago Pile-1, the first nuclear reactor.
Chicago Pile-1 achieved the controlled chain reaction in 1942.
Ole Romer made the first successful measurement of the speed of light.
Ole Romer made the measurement in 1676.
Ole Romer used observations of Jupiter’s moon Io in measuring the speed of light.
John Dalton proposed the first modern atomic theory.
John Dalton proposed the first modern atomic theory in 1808.
J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897.
Rutherford proposed the first nuclear model of the atom.
Rutherford proposed the first nuclear model of the atom in 1911.
Max Planck proposed the first quantum hypothesis.
Max Planck proposed the first quantum hypothesis in 1900.
Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley developed the first transistor.
The first transistor was developed in 1947.
The earliest known telescopes date to 1608.
Hans Lippershey is associated with the earliest known telescopes.
Galileo improved the earliest known telescopes.
Galileo used improved telescopes for astronomy.
Daniel Bernoulli proposed the earliest model of the kinetic theory of gases.
Daniel Bernoulli proposed the model in 1738.
Aristotle proposed the earliest effective theory of physics.
Thales of Miletus proposed the earliest natural philosophy.
Archimedes’ principle is the oldest known physical law that is still valid.
Gravity is the oldest fundamental force concept still used.
The Large Hadron Collider is the largest particle accelerator in energy and size.
The Large Hadron Collider is located at CERN.
The top quark is the largest fundamental particle by mass.
The mass of the top quark is approximately 172.5 GeV/c².
The Observable Universe is the largest known structure.
Ganymede is the largest moon of Jupiter.
Ganymede is a Galilean moon of Jupiter.
The neutrino is the smallest fundamental particle by mass, within the stated upper limit.
The Planck length is the smallest theoretically measurable length.
The Planck length is approximately 1.6 × 10⁻³⁵ m.
The elementary charge is the smallest charge.
The symbol for the elementary charge is e.
An electron has the elementary charge.
A proton has the elementary charge.
The Planck time is the smallest theoretically measurable time.
The Planck time is approximately 5.4 × 10⁻⁴⁴ s.
The speed of light is the highest possible speed.
The symbol for the speed of light is c.
The speed of light in vacuum is 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
The Large Hadron Collider is the highest-energy particle accelerator.
Quark-gluon plasma is the highest temperature achieved in a laboratory.
Quark-gluon plasma has been achieved at the Large Hadron Collider and RHIC.
Gamma rays are the highest-frequency electromagnetic radiation.
Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature.
The ground state is the lowest energy state of an atom.
Radio waves are the lowest-frequency electromagnetic radiation.
The speed of light is the fastest speed in nature.
The Helios probes and Parker Solar Probe are the fastest man-made objects relative to the Sun.
Near-light-speed protons and electrons are the fastest particles in accelerators.
Near-light-speed protons and electrons are found in the LHC and LEP.

rows.title: #2 · Physics: Extremes and Fundamental Limits
sub: Group-I F18: Science and Technology - Nature and Scope, Relevance to Daily Life, National S&T Policy

x: Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #2, pages 4-6
Massive particles can have speeds approaching zero in a rest frame.
Radioactive decay of some ultra-long-lived isotopes is among the slowest known processes.
Radio waves have the longest wavelength among electromagnetic radiation.
The proton is the longest-lived stable particle.
The experimental lower limit for the proton lifetime is greater than 10³⁴ years.
Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength among electromagnetic radiation.
The strong nuclear force has a range of approximately 10⁻¹⁵ metres.
The Planck time is the shortest theoretical time.
The maximum speed is c, the speed of light.
The Carnot efficiency is the maximum efficiency of a heat engine.
The threshold wavelength is the maximum wavelength for the photoelectric effect.
The threshold wavelength is given by λ₀ = hc/φ.
The work function φ is the minimum energy required to eject an electron.
The Heisenberg uncertainty principle gives the minimum uncertainty product as Δx·Δp ≥ ℏ/2.
The top quark is the most massive fundamental particle.
Neutrinos or photons are the most abundant particles in the Universe, depending on the context.
The strong nuclear force is the most powerful force at short range.
The neutrino is the least massive fundamental particle, while the photon has zero mass.
The intergalactic medium is the least dense form of ordinary matter.
Alpha particles are the least penetrating radiation.

The Celsius scale uses °C as its unit.
The Kelvin scale uses K as its unit.
The Fahrenheit scale uses °F as its unit.
The SI standard for length is the metre.
The metre is defined as the distance travelled by light in vacuum in 1/299792458 second.
The SI standard for mass is the kilogram.
The kilogram is defined using the fixed value of Planck constant h = 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
The SI standard for time is the second.
The second is defined as 9192631770 periods of radiation from the Cs-133 hyperfine transition.
The SI standard for electric current is the ampere.
The ampere is defined using the fixed elementary charge e = 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
The SI standard for temperature is the kelvin.
The kelvin is defined using the fixed Boltzmann constant k = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K.
The SI standard for amount of substance is the mole.
The mole is defined using the fixed Avogadro constant N_A = 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
The SI standard for luminous intensity is the candela.
The candela is defined using a fixed luminous efficacy of 683 lm/W for 540 THz radiation.

An optical fibre is used in telecommunication, endoscopy, and internet cables.
A solar cell is used in solar panels, calculators, and satellites.
An LED is used in displays, indicators, lighting, and optical communication.
A diode is used in rectifiers, voltage regulation with a Zener diode, and signal detection.
A transistor is used in amplifiers, switches, computers, and radios.

A generator or dynamo converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.
A transformer transfers electrical energy between high voltage and low voltage without net energy conversion.
A solar cell converts solar light into electrical energy.
An LED or bulb converts electrical energy into light and heat.

A microphone converts sound into electrical energy.
A photocell converts light into electrical energy.
A battery or cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy.

An optical fibre contains a core.

A manometer measures pressure difference or gas pressure.
A spectrometer measures wavelength, refractive index, and spectrum.

Household wiring has individual circuit fuses.

Inverters are used in solar power systems.

An inverter produces alternating voltage for AC appliances.

Wireless charging uses electromagnetic induction for mobile phones.
Wireless charging uses electromagnetic induction for electric vehicles.

Light exhibits particle nature through photons.
The wave nature of light explains interference.
The wave nature of light explains diffraction.
The wave nature of light explains polarisation.
The particle nature of light explains the photoelectric effect.
The particle nature of light explains the Compton effect.
Electromagnetic waves do not require a medium.
Light travels at its maximum speed in vacuum, denoted by c.
A transparent medium allows light to pass through it.
A translucent medium partially allows light to pass through it.
Frosted glass is a translucent medium.
Butter paper is a translucent medium.
An opaque medium does not allow light to pass through it.
A medium with a higher refractive index is optically denser.
The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in the same plane according to the first law of reflection.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection according to the second law of reflection.
The normal is perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence.
A regular or specular reflection occurs from a smooth surface.
A regular or specular reflection produces a clear image.
A mirror produces regular or specular reflection.
An irregular or diffused reflection occurs from a rough surface.
An irregular or diffused reflection does not produce a clear image.
A wall produces irregular or diffused reflection.
Paper produces irregular or diffused reflection.
Total internal reflection occurs when the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle for light travelling from a denser to a rarer medium.
A plane mirror forms a virtual image.
A plane mirror forms an erect image.
A plane mirror forms an image of the same size as the object.
A plane mirror laterally inverts an image.
A concave mirror forms a real and inverted image when the object is beyond C.
A concave mirror forms a virtual and erect image when the object is within F.
A convex mirror always forms a virtual image.
A convex mirror always forms an erect image.
A convex mirror forms a diminished image.
A plane mirror is used as a looking glass.
A plane mirror is used in a periscope.
A plane mirror is used in a kaleidoscope.
A concave mirror is used as a shaving mirror.
A concave mirror is used in headlights.
A concave mirror is used in a solar cooker.
A concave mirror is used in a telescope.
A convex mirror is used as a rear-view mirror.
A convex mirror is used as a security mirror.
A convex mirror is used in street lamps.
A shaving or makeup mirror produces a magnified erect image when the object is within F.
A headlight reflector produces a parallel beam when the bulb is at the focus.
A solar cooker or furnace converges sun rays at the focus.
A torch or searchlight produces a strong parallel beam.
A dentist mirror produces a magnified image of teeth.
A reflecting telescope has a large aperture.
A reflecting telescope has no chromatic aberration.
A vehicle rear-view mirror provides a wide field of view.
A vehicle rear-view mirror produces an erect diminished image.
A security or shop mirror provides large-area coverage.
A street-light reflector diverges light over a larger area.
A mirror used in an ATM or parking area provides a wider view for safety.
A plane-mirror image is virtual and erect.
A plane-mirror image has the same size as the object.
The image distance in a plane mirror equals the object distance.
A plane mirror laterally inverts an image by reversing left and right.
The magnification of a plane mirror is m = +1.
Refraction is caused by a change in the speed of light.
Light travels at different speeds in different media.
Refraction is associated with a change in wavelength.
The frequency of light remains the same during refraction.
The wavelength of light changes during refraction.
Refraction occurs because of an optical-density difference between media.
Prisms produce deviation and dispersion of light.
Objects in water appear raised because of apparent depth.
The critical angle is the angle of incidence in a denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90°.
The critical angle is denoted by C.
Critical-angle conditions require light to travel from a denser to a rarer medium.
The critical angle depends on the pair of media.
The critical angle also depends slightly on wavelength.
Total internal reflection is the basis of TIR devices.
An optical fibre keeps light inside its core.
Diamond brilliance results from multiple total internal reflections.
A Porro prism or binocular produces image inversion without loss.
An endoscope is used for medical viewing.
Total internal reflection requires light to travel from an optically denser to a rarer medium.
Total internal reflection requires the angle of incidence to exceed the critical angle, i > C.
Total internal reflection reflects the entire light back into the denser medium.
Total internal reflection produces no refraction in the ideal case.
Total internal reflection produces 100% reflection in the ideal case.
Optical fibres are used for communication and endoscopy.
Diamond sparkle is associated with a very small critical angle of approximately 24.4°.
A mirage is caused by atmospheric total internal reflection.
Prisms in binoculars or periscopes reflect light without silvering.
Reflectors in road signs provide high visibility.
Dew drops sparkle because of optical reflection effects.
The core of an optical fibre has a higher refractive index than its cladding.
The cladding of an optical fibre has a lower refractive index than its core.
The angle of incidence at the core-cladding interface must satisfy i > C.
Optical fibres are immune to interference.
Optical fibres are used in telecommunication.
Optical fibres are used in medical endoscopy.
Medical endoscopy uses optical fibres to view internal organs.
Optical fibres are used for precise laser delivery in surgery.
Optical fibres provide lightweight data transmission in military and aircraft applications.
An endoscope works through a bundle of optical fibres using total internal reflection.
An endoscope has one fibre bundle for illumination.
An endoscope has one fibre bundle for image transmission.
An endoscope is flexible enough to be inserted into body cavities.
An endoscope permits non-invasive or minimally invasive viewing.
An inferior mirage occurs in a desert.
An inferior mirage is caused by total internal reflection due to hot air near the ground.
Hot air near the ground has a lower refractive index.
A superior mirage is caused by total internal reflection due to cold air layers.
A mirage is caused by a continuous decrease or increase of refractive index with height.
A mirage can appear as an inverted image of a distant object.
An inferior mirage can have a water-like appearance.
Diamond has a very high refractive index of approximately 2.42.
Diamond has a very small critical angle of approximately 24.4°.
Most light in diamond undergoes total internal reflection.
Diamond brilliance and fire are caused by total internal reflection and dispersion.
Diamond facets are designed to maximise total internal reflection.
A convex lens is thicker at the centre.
A double-convex lens is a type of convex lens.
A plano-convex lens is a type of convex lens.
A concavo-convex lens is a type of convex lens.
A concave lens is thicker at the edges.
A double-concave lens is a type of concave lens.
A plano-concave lens is a type of concave lens.
A convexo-concave lens is a type of concave lens.
A bifocal or progressive lens combines two powers.
A convex lens forms a real, inverted, diminished image when the object is beyond 2F.
A convex lens forms a real, inverted, same-sized image when the object is at 2F.
A convex lens forms a real, inverted, magnified image when the object is between F and 2F.
A convex lens forms a real, inverted, highly magnified image when the object is at F.
A convex lens forms the image at infinity when the object is at F.
A convex lens forms a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is within F.
A concave lens forms a virtual, erect, diminished image for any object position.
A convex lens is used as a magnifying glass.
A convex lens is used in a camera.
A convex lens is used in a microscope.
A convex lens is used in a telescope.
A convex lens is used in a projector.
The eye lens is a convex lens.
A concave lens is used in spectacles for myopia.
A concave lens is used in a peephole.
A concave lens is used in door viewers.
A combination of lenses is used in microscopes.
A combination of lenses is used in telescopes.
A combination of lenses is used in binoculars.
A magnifying glass produces a virtual magnified image when the object is within F.
A camera forms a real inverted image on film or a sensor.
A microscope objective forms a real image.
A telescope objective forms a real image.
A projector forms a magnified real image on a screen.
The human eye forms a real image on the retina.
A burning glass converges sun rays.
A concave lens corrects myopia by diverging rays so that the image forms on the retina.
A peephole or door viewer provides a wide field of view.
Some Galileo telescopes use a concave lens as an eyepiece.
A lens combination can correct certain aberrations.
The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres.
The unit of lens power is the dioptre.
The symbol for dioptre is D.
A convex lens has positive power.
A concave lens has negative power.
The cornea provides the main refraction in the human eye.
The cornea contributes approximately 70% of the focusing.
The iris controls the amount of light entering the eye.
The pupil is the aperture for light entry.
The eye lens performs fine focusing through accommodation.
Ciliary muscles change the curvature of the eye lens.
The retina is the screen where the image is formed.
The retina contains rods and cones.
The optic nerve carries signals to the brain.
Aqueous humour helps maintain the shape of the eye.
Vitreous humour helps maintain the shape of the eye.
Distant objects appear blurred in myopia.
Nearby objects appear blurred in hypermetropia.
Presbyopia is an age-related loss of accommodation.
Astigmatism produces a distorted image due to irregular curvature.
A cataract is clouding of the eye lens.
Colour blindness is a genetic defect in cones.
Myopia is caused by an elongated eyeball or excessive converging power.
Myopia forms the image in front of the retina.
Myopia is corrected with a concave diverging lens.
A myopia-correcting lens has negative power, such as –2 D.
A concave lens diverges rays so that the image falls on the retina in myopia.
Hypermetropia is caused by a shortened eyeball or insufficient converging power.
Hypermetropia forms the image behind the retina.
Hypermetropia is corrected with a convex converging lens.
A hypermetropia-correcting lens has positive power, such as +2 D.
A convex lens converges rays so that the image falls on the retina in hypermetropia.
Presbyopia is caused by weakening of the ciliary muscles.
Presbyopia is caused by loss of lens flexibility with age.
Presbyopia causes the near point to recede.
Presbyopia is corrected with bifocal or progressive lenses.
The near portion of a presbyopia-correcting lens is convex.
Presbyopia can involve a combination of myopia and hypermetropia in old age.
Astigmatism is caused by irregular curvature of the cornea or lens.
Astigmatism involves different powers in different meridians.
Astigmatism causes blurred or distorted vision at all distances.
Astigmatism is corrected with a cylindrical lens.
Toric contact lenses can correct astigmatism.
The near point is the closest distance at which the eye can see clearly.
The normal near point is 25 cm.
The normal near point is called the least distance of distinct vision.
The near point in myopia is closer than 25 cm.
The near point in hypermetropia is farther than 25 cm.
The near point in presbyopia is farther than 25 cm.
The far point is the farthest distance at which the eye can see clearly.
The normal far point is infinity.
The far point in myopia is finite.
The far point in myopia is closer than infinity.
The far point in hypermetropia is infinity.
Hypermetropia affects near vision despite an infinite far point.
Accommodation is the ability of the eye to focus objects at different distances.
Ciliary muscles change the curvature of the eye lens during accommodation.
The lens becomes thicker for near vision.
A thicker lens is more converging.
The lens becomes thinner for distant vision.
The accommodation range extends from the near point of 25 cm to the far point at infinity.
The main phenomena in a rainbow are dispersion, total internal reflection, and refraction.
Sunlight enters a water drop and disperses.
Sunlight undergoes total internal reflection at the back of a water drop.
The dispersed light refracts out of the water drop.
A primary rainbow involves one total internal reflection.
A primary rainbow has red on the outer side.
A primary rainbow has violet on the inner side.
A secondary rainbow involves two total internal reflections.
A secondary rainbow has reversed colours.
A secondary rainbow is fainter than a primary rainbow.
The Sun is behind the observer during rainbow formation.
Water drops are in front of the observer during rainbow formation.
Dispersion occurs because different wavelengths have different refractive indices.
Violet has the highest refractive index in the visible spectrum.
Red has the lowest refractive index in the visible spectrum.
In a primary rainbow, red is outermost.
In a primary rainbow, violet is innermost.
The visible spectrum is represented by VIBGYOR.
A prism spectrometer produces a pure spectrum.
A rainbow is a natural spectrum.
Chromatic aberration is a defect in lenses.
An achromatic doublet minimises chromatic aberration.
Diamond fire is caused by dispersion of white light.
Rayleigh scattering is produced by particles much smaller than the wavelength.
Mie scattering is produced by larger particles.
Dust and air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths more strongly.
Blue and violet are scattered the most in the atmosphere.
Blue and violet have the highest frequencies among the relevant visible colours.
The human eye is more sensitive to blue than violet.
The sky therefore appears blue to the human eye.
Scattered light reaches the eye from all directions.
Sunlight travels a greater distance through the atmosphere at sunset.
Blue light is scattered away during sunset.
The remaining red or orange light reaches the eye at sunset.
Pollution and dust enhance the red colour of a sunset.
Twinkling stars are caused by atmospheric refraction.
Air-density variations cause continuous changes in refractive index.
Atmospheric refraction causes random apparent positions of stars.
The apparent intensity of a star fluctuates during twinkling.
Planets do not twinkle because they appear as discs.
The disc appearance of planets produces an averaging effect.
Twinkling of stars is caused by atmospheric refraction.
Advance sunrise is caused by atmospheric refraction.
Delayed sunset is caused by atmospheric refraction.
Atmospheric refraction accounts for approximately two minutes of advance sunrise or delayed sunset.
The apparent position of stars is affected by atmospheric refraction.
A rainbow is caused by dispersion and total internal reflection in water drops.
A blue sky and red sunset are caused by Rayleigh scattering.
A mirage is caused by total internal reflection.
An eclipse is caused by shadow formation.
Shadow formation in an eclipse results from rectilinear propagation of light.

rows.title: #19 · Sound, Ultrasound and Musical Acoustics
sub: Group-I F18: Science and Technology - Nature and Scope, Relevance to Daily Life, National S&T Policy

x: Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #19, pages 76-81
Sound can travel through solids, liquids, and gases.
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
Sound propagates through compressions and rarefactions.
The speed of sound is generally greatest in solids.
The speed of sound is generally lower in liquids than in solids.
The speed of sound is generally lowest in gases.
The approximate speed of sound in air at 20–25°C is 340–343 m/s.
The approximate speed of sound in water at 20–25°C is 1480–1500 m/s.
The approximate speed of sound in steel or iron at 20–25°C is 5000–6000 m/s.
The approximate speed of sound in glass at 20–25°C is 5000–6000 m/s.
The speed of sound in a vacuum is zero.
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because a material medium is absent.
The frequency of sound is the number of vibrations per second.
The frequency of sound is the number of compressions per second.
The unit of frequency is hertz (Hz).
Frequency determines the pitch of sound.
The human audible frequency range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
The wavelength of sound is the distance between two successive compressions or rarefactions.
Higher frequency corresponds to smaller wavelength.
The wavelength of a 20 Hz sound in air at 340 m/s is 17 m.
The wavelength of a 20 kHz sound in air at 340 m/s is 1.7 cm.
The amplitude of sound is the maximum displacement of particles from their mean position.
Amplitude determines the loudness of sound.
Amplitude determines the intensity of sound.
The energy of sound is proportional to the square of its amplitude.
The unit of amplitude is metre (m).
Amplitude has no effect on the speed of sound.
Amplitude has no effect on frequency.
Amplitude has no effect on pitch.
Pitch is directly proportional to frequency.
Low frequency produces a bass or deep sound.
A male voice is an example of a bass or deep sound.
High frequency produces a shrill sound.
A female voice is an example of a shrill sound.
A whistle is an example of a shrill sound.
Pitch is the sensation of frequency in the brain.
Loudness is directly related to amplitude.
Loudness is the sensation of intensity or amplitude.
The unit of loudness is decibel (dB).
Quality or timbre distinguishes two sounds having the same pitch and loudness.
Quality or timbre depends on the waveform present.
Quality or timbre depends on the overtones present.
Quality or timbre depends on the harmonics present.
The same note played on a flute, violin, and piano sounds different.
A sound with more overtones has richer quality.
Quality is determined by the shape of the periodic waveform.
The speed of sound increases with an increase in temperature.
The speed of sound increases by approximately 0.61 m/s per 1°C rise in temperature.
The speed of sound at 0°C is approximately 331 m/s.
The speed of sound at 20°C is approximately 343 m/s.
Sound travels fastest through solids because solids have high elasticity or bulk modulus.
The molecules in solids are closely packed.
Sound travels at an intermediate speed through liquids.
Liquids are less elastic than solids.
The molecules in gases are far apart.
The order of sound speed is solid > liquid > gas in general.
A train sound is heard better through rails than through air.
The audible sound range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
The audible sound range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
Infrasonic sound has a frequency below 20 Hz.
Ultrasonic sound has a frequency above 20 kHz.
The human hearing limit decreases with age.
Age-related hearing loss especially affects higher frequencies.
Human hearing is most sensitive around 2000–4000 Hz.
Ultrasound is used for medical imaging.
Ultrasound is used for cleaning delicate parts and jewellery.
Ultrasound is used in industry to detect cracks or flaws in metals.
SONAR uses ultrasound for underwater detection.
Ultrasound is used for pest control.
Ultrasound can drive away insects and rodents.
Ultrasound is used for welding and drilling in precision machining.
Infrasound is used for earthquake detection.
Infrasound is used for monitoring weather.
Infrasound can detect storms and tornadoes.
Infrasound is used by the military to detect nuclear explosions and missiles.
Animals can sense infrasound before natural disasters.
Infrasound is used in the study of the atmosphere.
SONAR stands for Sound Navigation And Ranging.
SONAR works on the echo method.
SONAR works by reflection of ultrasonic waves.
SONAR sends ultrasonic pulses toward an object.
The ultrasonic pulses are reflected by the object.
SONAR measures the time interval between sending and receiving the reflected pulse.
SONAR uses ultrasound as its wave.
SONAR is used to detect submarines.
Submarine detection is a military use of SONAR.
SONAR locates fish for the fishing industry.
SONAR supports underwater navigation by ships and submarines.
SONAR locates wrecks and sunken ships or objects.
SONAR has limited use in underwater communication.
An echo is used in SONAR for distance and depth measurement.
Medical ultrasound uses echoes to image internal organs.
Radar uses a principle similar to echolocation.
Echo time is used to measure the speed of sound.
Echoes are relevant to architectural acoustics.
Architectural acoustics involves designing halls for reverberation control.
The minimum distance required for an echo is 17.2 m.
The 17.2 m minimum echo distance is based on the human ear's persistence of hearing of 0.1 s.
The Doppler effect is the apparent change in frequency due to relative motion between a source and an observer.
An approaching source produces a higher apparent frequency for the observer.
An approaching source produces a higher apparent pitch.
A receding source produces a lower apparent frequency for the observer.
A receding source produces a lower apparent pitch.
The Doppler effect is used in radar guns.
The Doppler effect is used in medical Doppler applications.
The Doppler effect is used in astronomy for light.
String instruments include the guitar, sitar, and violin.
String instruments produce sound through vibration of strings.
The strings of string instruments vibrate as transverse standing waves.
Wind instruments include the flute, clarinet, and shehnai.
Wind instruments produce sound through vibration of an air column.
The air column in wind instruments vibrates as a longitudinal standing wave.
Membrane instruments include the tabla and drum.
Membrane instruments produce sound through vibration of a stretched membrane.
Plate instruments include cymbals and bells.
Plate instruments produce sound through vibration of plates or solids.
Electronic oscillators and speakers are listed as musical instruments.
The pitch of a musical instrument is controlled by the frequency of vibration.
The frequency of a string instrument depends on the length of the string.
The frequency of a string instrument depends on the tension of the string.
The frequency of a string instrument depends on the thickness of the string.
The frequency of a wind instrument depends on the length of its air column.
The loudness of a musical instrument is controlled by the amplitude of vibration.
The amplitude of vibration depends on the force of striking or blowing.
The quality or timbre of a musical instrument is controlled by its overtones or harmonics.
The overtones or harmonics depend on the shape and material of the instrument.
A closed pipe produces only odd harmonics.
An open pipe produces all harmonics.

Waves are classified based on medium into mechanical waves and electromagnetic waves.
Waves are classified based on the direction of vibration into transverse waves and longitudinal waves.
Waves are classified based on energy propagation into progressive waves and stationary waves.
Waves are classified based on dimension into one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and three-dimensional waves.
Matter waves are associated with de Broglie.
Shock waves are another type of wave.
Mechanical waves require a material medium.
A material medium for mechanical waves may be a solid, liquid, or gas.
Electromagnetic waves do not require a medium.
Electromagnetic waves can travel in a vacuum.
Matter waves are associated with moving particles.
Matter waves do not need a medium.
Sound waves require a material medium.
Light waves can travel in a vacuum.
Sound waves in air are longitudinal waves.
Waves on a string are transverse waves.
Water surface waves are transverse waves.
Seismic P-waves and S-waves are both longitudinal and transverse waves.
Waves in a spring or slinky can be longitudinal or transverse waves.
Radio waves have wavelengths greater than 1 metre.
Microwaves have wavelengths from 1 millimetre to 1 metre.
Infrared waves have wavelengths from 700 nanometres to 1 millimetre.
Visible light has wavelengths from 400 to 700 nanometres.
Ultraviolet waves have wavelengths from 10 to 400 nanometres.
X-rays have wavelengths from 0.01 to 10 nanometres.
Gamma rays have wavelengths less than 0.01 nanometre.
Waves on a string are mechanical waves.
Water surface waves are mechanical waves.
Sound waves in air are longitudinal waves.
Sound waves in air travel through gas.
P-waves travel through solids, liquids, and gases.
Waves in a spring are compression waves in a solid.
Ultrasonic waves are longitudinal waves in various media.
Energy is proportional to the square of amplitude.
Intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude.
Amplitude has no effect on wave speed.
Amplitude has no effect on frequency.
Amplitude has no effect on wavelength.
Velocity is independent of frequency in the same medium.
Velocity changes with the properties of different media.
The speed of light is the same for all frequencies in a vacuum.
At the same frequency, higher velocity produces a longer wavelength.
In the same medium, velocity is constant and wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency.
Sound travels faster in solids than in other listed media.
At the same frequency, faster sound has a longer wavelength.
Waves transfer energy without transferring matter.
Wave energy is proportional to the square of amplitude multiplied by the square of frequency.
Intensity is power per unit area.
Intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude.
Mechanical-wave energy comes from particle oscillation.
Electromagnetic-wave energy comes from oscillating electric and magnetic fields.
Sound waves are used for communication.
Sound waves are used in sonar.
Sound waves are used in medical ultrasound.
Light waves are used for vision.
Light waves are used in optical fibres.
Light waves are used in lasers.
Radio waves are used in broadcasting.
Radio waves are used in mobile communication.
Microwaves are used in satellite communication.
X-rays are used in medical imaging.
X-rays are used in security scanning.
Ultrasonic waves are used for cleaning.
Ultrasonic waves are used in echocardiography.
Ultrasonic waves are used for ranging.
Young’s double-slit experiment demonstrates constructive and destructive interference of light.
Colours in soap bubbles and oil films are examples of thin-film interference.
Beats in sound result from interference of two close frequencies.
Noise-cancelling headphones use destructive interference of sound.
Bending of light around an obstacle allows light to enter the geometrical shadow.
Sound can be heard around corners because sound waves diffract easily.
Sound waves diffract easily because they have long wavelengths.
A single-slit diffraction pattern has a central bright fringe and secondary fringes.
Light cannot be seen clearly around corners because light has a very small wavelength.
Polaroid sunglasses reduce glare by cutting reflected light.
Three-dimensional movies use separate images for each eye.
LCD screens use polarization to control light transmission.
Stress analysis uses photoelasticity to show stress patterns.
Optical activity is used to measure the concentration of solutions.
Communication uses polarization multiplexing in optical fibres.
Radar speed guns measure vehicle speed using the Doppler effect.
Medical Doppler ultrasound measures blood-flow velocity.
Astronomy uses red shift and blue shift to study the expanding universe and star motion.
SONAR measures the speed of submarines and underwater objects using the Doppler effect.
Weather radar detects storms and wind speed.
Bats use echolocation with frequency shifts for navigation.

Heat is a form of energy that flows due to a temperature difference.
Temperature measures the hotness or coldness of a body.
Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of molecules.
Heat flows from a higher temperature to a lower temperature.
There is no net heat flow when two bodies have the same temperature.
Bodies with the same temperature are in thermal equilibrium.
The SI unit of heat or energy is the joule (J).
One calorie is equal to 4.186 joules, approximately 4.2 joules.
One kilocalorie is equal to 4186 joules.
The mechanical equivalent of heat is 4.186 joules per calorie.
The Celsius scale has an ice point of 0°C.
The Celsius scale has a steam point of 100°C.
The symbol of the Celsius scale is °C.
The Kelvin scale is an absolute scale.
The ice point on the Kelvin scale is 273.15 K.
The symbol of the Kelvin scale is K.
The Fahrenheit scale has an ice point of 32°F.
The Fahrenheit scale has a steam point of 212°F.
The symbol of the Fahrenheit scale is °F.
The Rankine scale is an absolute Fahrenheit scale.
The symbol of the Rankine scale is °R.
The Kelvin temperature is equal to the Celsius temperature plus 273.15.
The approximate conversion from Celsius to Kelvin is K = °C + 273.
A temperature of 27°C is equal to approximately 300 K.
A temperature of 0°C is equal to approximately 273 K.
A temperature of –273°C is equal to approximately 0 K.
Conduction transfers heat through direct contact.
Conduction does not involve bulk motion.
Convection transfers heat by the actual movement of fluid particles.
Radiation transfers heat by electromagnetic waves.
Radiation does not require a medium.
A metal spoon placed in hot tea becomes hot through conduction.
Heating one end of a metal rod causes the other end to become hot through conduction.
Metal bases of cooking utensils conduct heat to food.
Wood and plastic provide insulation because they are poor conductors.
Boiling water demonstrates convection because hot water rises and cold water sinks.
Sea breeze and land breeze result from air movement due to a temperature difference.
Room heaters and air conditioners circulate air by convection.
Hot air balloons rise because hot air rises.
Heat from the Sun reaches Earth through a vacuum by radiation.
Radiation allows a person to feel heat from a fire or heater without touching it.
A black body is a perfect absorber of radiation.
A black body is a perfect emitter of radiation.
Shiny walls in a thermos flask minimize radiation loss.
Liquids and gases provide the medium for convection.
Radiation can occur without a medium.
Radiation can occur in a vacuum.
Railway tracks have gaps left for thermal expansion.
Bridges use rollers or expansion joints to allow thermal expansion.
Thermometers use liquid expansion to measure temperature.
Bimetallic strips are used in thermostats.
Bimetallic strips are used in electric irons.
Bimetallic strips are used in fire alarms.
Hot rivets contract on cooling and form a tight joint.
Overflow pipes in tanks allow for the expansion of liquid.
Water contracts when heated from 0°C to 4°C.
Water has its maximum density at 4°C.
The density of water decreases below 4°C.
The density of water decreases above 4°C.
Lakes and ponds freeze from the top, allowing aquatic life to survive.
The volume of water is minimum at 4°C.
Water is used as a coolant because its high specific heat allows it to absorb large heat with a small temperature change.
Coastal areas have a moderate climate because of the high specific heat of water.
Water in hot water bottles retains heat for a longer time.
Land has a lower specific heat than sea water.
Land heats and cools faster than sea water.
Substances with high specific heat cook more slowly.
Ice provides cooling because its high latent heat of fusion allows it to absorb a large amount of heat.
Steam causes more severe burns than boiling water because of its high latent heat of vaporisation.
Refrigeration uses latent heat absorbed during evaporation.
Evaporation of perspiration cools the body.
Latent heat is released during condensation in the formation of clouds and rain.
The latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg.
The latent heat of fusion of ice is 80 cal/g.
The temperature remains constant during melting at the melting point.
The melting point of ice is 0°C at 1 atmosphere pressure.
The latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg.
The latent heat of vaporisation of water is 540 cal/g.
The temperature remains constant during boiling at the boiling point.
The boiling point of water is 100°C at 1 atmosphere pressure.
The boiling point increases when pressure increases.
Evaporation occurs when faster molecules escape from a liquid.
The escape of faster molecules decreases the average kinetic energy of the remaining molecules.
The decrease in average kinetic energy of the remaining molecules causes cooling.
Sweating cools the body through evaporation.
Water in an earthen pot cools through evaporation.
Desert coolers use evaporation for cooling.
Boiling is different from evaporation because evaporation is a surface phenomenon occurring at all temperatures.
A refrigerator extracts heat from the cold body inside and rejects heat to the hot surroundings.
The refrigeration cycle consists of evaporation, compression, condensation, and expansion.
Refrigeration is based on the Second Law of Thermodynamics.
External work is required for refrigeration.
Liquid refrigerant evaporates at low pressure.
Evaporation of the liquid refrigerant absorbs latent heat.
Earlier CFC refrigerants have been phased out.
A desirable refrigerant has a low boiling point.
A desirable refrigerant has high latent heat.
A refrigerant absorbs heat during evaporation.
A refrigerant releases heat during condensation.
A heat engine converts heat energy into mechanical work.
A heat engine absorbs heat from a source.
A heat engine does work after absorbing heat from the source.
A heat engine rejects heat to a sink.
A heat engine requires a hot source.
A heat engine requires a cold sink.
A heat engine requires a working substance.
A heat engine is based on the First Law and Second Law of Thermodynamics.
Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature.
Molecular motion is minimum at absolute zero.
Absolute zero is unattainable according to the Third Law of Thermodynamics.
For an ideal gas, volume theoretically becomes zero at absolute zero.
For an ideal gas, pressure theoretically becomes zero at absolute zero.
Absolute zero is the starting point of the Kelvin scale.

An object floats when its density is less than the liquid’s density.

A lactometer measures the relative density of liquids.
Ships and submarines control average density using ballast.
Hydraulic brakes transmit pressure equally to all wheels.
A hydraulic jack lifts heavy vehicles.
Pressure applied at one end of a syringe is transmitted to the other end.

Bulldozers use hydraulic systems for force amplification.

Submarines control buoyancy using ballast tanks.

A hydrometer measures the density of liquids.
A lactometer checks the purity of milk.

Pressure at the bottom of a submerged object is greater than pressure at the top.
The net upward buoyant force is caused by higher hydrostatic pressure at greater depth.

Only a small part of an iceberg remains above water.
The density of ice is less than the density of water.
A fish bladder controls buoyancy for depth regulation.
Heated air has lower density in a hot-air balloon.
Lower-density heated air produces a net upward force in a hot-air balloon.
The surface of water acts like an elastic membrane for a water strider or insect walking on water.
Small liquid drops have a spherical shape.

Surface tension supports the weight of a razor blade floating on water.
Two surfaces in a soap bubble produce higher excess pressure.
Capillary rise or fall produces meniscus formation.

Reduced surface tension gives detergents and soaps better cleaning action.
Capillary action makes water rise against gravity in plants.
Medicine droppers are associated with the formation of drops.
Ink pens are associated with the formation of drops.
Molten metals form a spherical shape in space.
Molten metals form a spherical shape in powder metallurgy.
Lung surfactants reduce surface tension in alveoli.
Water rises in a narrow glass tube.

Melting of ice and melting of wax do not form a new substance.

Freezing of water changes a liquid into a solid.

Dissolving sugar in water forms a solution.

The composition changes during a chemical change.

A chemical change is usually irreversible.

A chemical change involves significant energy absorbed or released as heat or light.

Photosynthesis is important for food production.

Neutralisation is used in industrial processes.
Electrolysis of water uses electric current to decompose water.
Electrolysis of water is used to produce hydrogen and oxygen.

Drought is also called a creeping emergency.
Drought is a serious shortfall in the availability of water.
Drought mainly affects agriculture, drinking-water supply, and industry.
In India, drought is mainly caused by the inadequacy and uneven distribution of rainfall.
More than 80% of India’s rainfall is received in less than 100 days during the southwest monsoon.
Large parts of India depend on rain-fed agriculture and are vulnerable to drought.
Excess withdrawal of groundwater over replenishment aggravates drought in the long run.
Surface-water availability itself becomes scarce in Peninsular India during years of insufficient rainfall.
The Arthashastra devoted a section to mitigation measures for combating famines in the 4th century B.C.
After Independence, drought-relief works were undertaken in severely affected areas.
The Green Revolution in the late 1960s reduced the necessity for famine-relief work.
The Drought Prone Areas Programme was taken up as a holistic drought-management programme.
The Disaster Management Act, 2005 provided national-level disaster-management legislation.
Drought is a prolonged deficiency of rainfall or moisture leading to water scarcity.
Drought is a slow-onset natural disaster or creeping hazard.
Approximately 68% of India’s geographical area is drought-prone.
Chronically drought-prone areas receive less than 750 mm of rainfall.

Drought-prone areas receive 750–1125 mm of rainfall.
Drought-prone areas constitute approximately 35% of India’s area.

Hydrological drought involves the depletion of reservoirs, rivers, aquifers, and other surface-water and groundwater sources.

Socio-economic drought occurs when demand for water exceeds supply.

Socio-economic drought has a long-term time lag.

At least three triggers are required for drought declaration under the 2016 Manual for Drought Management.
Drought monitoring indicators include rainfall deviation, dry spells, NDVI, soil moisture, and reservoir and groundwater levels.
The State Disaster Response Fund is the primary fund for drought relief.
The National Disaster Response Fund is used in severe drought cases.
MGNREGA provides employment support in drought management.
PMFBY provides crop insurance in drought management.

An avalanche is a rapid flow of snow, ice, and debris down a mountain slope.
An avalanche is a geological and snow-related natural hazard.
Avalanches occur in India mainly in the Himalayan region.
Avalanches mainly occur in high-altitude areas.
The nodal ministry for avalanche management is the Ministry of Defence.
The key technical agency for avalanche management is the Defence Geoinformatics Research Establishment (DGRE).
The Defence Geoinformatics Research Establishment was earlier known as the Snow and Avalanche Study Establishment (SASE).
The Defence Geoinformatics Research Establishment functions under the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO).
A slab avalanche occurs when a large cohesive slab of snow breaks off and slides.
A slab avalanche is the most dangerous type of avalanche.
A loose snow avalanche, also called a sluff, consists of small slides of dry, powdery snow.
An ice avalanche involves ice masses from glaciers.
A rock or debris avalanche consists of a mixture of rock, soil, and snow.
Heavy snowfall is a natural cause of avalanches.
Weak snow layers caused by a temperature gradient are a natural cause of avalanches.
Steep slopes of 30°–45° are a natural cause of avalanches.
Earthquakes and seismic activity are natural causes of avalanches.
Wind loading is a natural cause of avalanches.
A rapid temperature rise is a natural cause of avalanches.
Rain falling on snow is a natural cause of avalanches.
Skiing is a human or other cause of avalanches.
Mountaineering is a human or other cause of avalanches.
Road construction is a human or other cause of avalanches.
Artificial triggering using explosives is a human or other cause of avalanches.
Deforestation is a human or other cause of avalanches.
Climate change effects are human or other causes of avalanches.
Jammu and Kashmir is the most affected region among the avalanche-prone areas of India.
Lahaul-Spiti in Himachal Pradesh is an avalanche-prone area.
Kinnaur in Himachal Pradesh is an avalanche-prone area.
Rohtang Pass in Himachal Pradesh is an avalanche-prone area.
Chamba in Himachal Pradesh is an avalanche-prone area.
The higher reaches of the Garhwal Himalaya in Uttarakhand are avalanche-prone.
The higher reaches of the Kumaon Himalaya in Uttarakhand are avalanche-prone.
Sikkim has high-altitude avalanche-prone Himalayan stretches.
Arunachal Pradesh has high-altitude avalanche-prone Himalayan stretches.
The DGRE undertakes avalanche hazard mapping.
The DGRE develops avalanche mitigation technologies.
The Border Roads Organisation (BRO) constructs roads in avalanche-prone areas.
The Border Roads Organisation maintains roads in avalanche-prone areas.
The Border Roads Organisation installs protection structures in avalanche-prone areas.
NDMA guidelines provide for avalanche risk zonation.
NDMA guidelines provide for avalanche early warning.
NDMA guidelines provide for structural avalanche mitigation measures.
NDMA guidelines provide for non-structural avalanche mitigation measures.
The DGRE issues daily avalanche warning bulletins during the winter season.
Snow bridges are structural measures for avalanche management.
Snow nets are structural measures for avalanche management.
Retaining walls are structural measures for avalanche management.
Galleries are structural measures for avalanche management.
Hazard zonation mapping is a non-structural measure for avalanche management.
Restricted movement is a non-structural measure for avalanche management.
Training is a non-structural measure for avalanche management.
Awareness is a non-structural measure for avalanche management.

Physical vulnerability is the susceptibility of buildings to disasters.
Physical vulnerability is the susceptibility of infrastructure to disasters.
Physical vulnerability is the susceptibility of physical assets to disasters.
Weak houses in earthquake zones are an example of physical vulnerability.
Settlements in floodplains are an example of physical vulnerability.
Social vulnerability is based on age.
Social vulnerability is based on gender.
Social vulnerability is based on caste.
Social vulnerability is based on disability.
Social vulnerability is based on social status.
Women are examples of groups facing social vulnerability.
Children are examples of groups facing social vulnerability.
Elderly people are examples of groups facing social vulnerability.
SC/ST communities are examples of groups facing social vulnerability.
Persons with disabilities are examples of groups facing social vulnerability.
Economic vulnerability includes a lack of livelihood options.
Daily wage workers are examples of groups facing economic vulnerability.
Small farmers are examples of groups facing economic vulnerability.
Informal sector workers are examples of groups facing economic vulnerability.
Environmental vulnerability results from the degradation of natural systems that increases risk.
Deforestation leading to landslides is an example of environmental vulnerability.
Loss of mangroves increasing cyclone impact is an example of environmental vulnerability.
Systemic or institutional vulnerability includes weak governance.
Systemic or institutional vulnerability includes poor coordination.
Systemic or institutional vulnerability includes a lack of preparedness.
Inadequate early warning systems are an example of systemic or institutional vulnerability.
Delayed response is an example of systemic or institutional vulnerability.
Children, especially unaccompanied children, are age-based vulnerable groups in India.
Elderly people are age-based vulnerable groups in India.
Women are gender-based vulnerable groups in India.
Pregnant women are gender-based vulnerable groups in India.
Lactating women are gender-based vulnerable groups in India.
Single women are gender-based vulnerable groups in India.
Widows are gender-based vulnerable groups in India.
Transgender persons are gender-based vulnerable groups in India.
Persons with Disabilities are disability-based vulnerable groups in India.
Persons with Disabilities are abbreviated as PwD.
Poor people are socio-economic vulnerable groups in India.
SC/ST communities are socio-economic vulnerable groups in India.
Informal sector workers are socio-economic vulnerable groups in India.
Homeless people are socio-economic vulnerable groups in India.
People living in high-risk zones are location-based vulnerable groups in India.
Coastal areas are high-risk zones for location-based vulnerability.
Seismic Zone V is a high-risk zone for location-based vulnerability.
Flood plains are high-risk zones for location-based vulnerability.
Hilly areas are high-risk zones for location-based vulnerability.
Migrants are vulnerable groups in India.
Refugees are vulnerable groups in India.
Remote tribal communities are vulnerable groups in India.
The NDMA focus area of disability-inclusive disaster risk reduction includes the NDMA Guidelines on Disability Inclusive Disaster Risk Reduction.

School safety under the NDMA focus areas has a special focus on children.
Gender mainstreaming under the NDMA focus areas includes women’s leadership in disaster risk reduction.

Women’s leadership and participation in disaster risk reduction are part of the PM’s 10-Point Agenda.
Minimum standards of relief include special provisions for vulnerable groups.
Community-based disaster risk reduction emphasizes including the most vulnerable in planning.

A heatwave is a period of abnormally high temperatures exceeding the normal maximum temperature during the summer season.
The heatwave season in India mainly extends from March to June.
The heatwave season in India sometimes extends to July.
The India Meteorological Department is the nodal agency for forecasting heatwaves.
The NDMA Guidelines for Preparation of Action Plan – Prevention and Management of Heat Wave provide key guidelines for heatwave management.
The NDMA Guidelines for Preparation of Action Plan – Prevention and Management of Heat Wave were updated in 2019.
Heatwave is included in the list of notified disasters eligible for SDRF and NDRF assistance as per the latest updates.
The minimum threshold temperature for declaring a heatwave in plains is 40°C.
A heatwave in plains is declared when the temperature departure from normal is 4.5°C to 6.4°C.
A severe heatwave in plains is declared when the temperature departure from normal is more than 6.4°C.
The minimum threshold temperature for declaring a heatwave in coastal areas is 37°C.
A heatwave in coastal areas is declared when the temperature departure from normal is 4.5°C or more.
The minimum threshold temperature for declaring a heatwave in hilly regions is 30°C.
A heatwave in hilly regions is declared when the temperature departure from normal is 4.5°C to 6.4°C.
A severe heatwave in hilly regions is declared when the temperature departure from normal is more than 6.4°C.
A heatwave in plains is also identified when the actual maximum temperature is at least 45°C.
A severe heatwave in plains is also identified when the actual maximum temperature is at least 47°C.
The green colour alert level indicates normal conditions.
The green colour alert level requires no action.
The yellow colour alert level indicates a heat alert.
The yellow colour alert level requires people to be updated and monitor conditions.
The orange colour alert level indicates a severe heat alert.
The orange colour alert level requires preparedness.
The red colour alert level indicates an extreme heat alert.
The red colour alert level requires action.
Heat Action Plans are prepared by states and cities with support from NDMA and IMD.
Cool roofs use reflective coatings or white painting of roofs.
The IMD provides early warning through colour-coded alerts.
Public awareness measures include communicating do’s and don’ts.
Public awareness measures include ORS distribution.
Public awareness measures include establishing cooling centres.
Structural measures include drinking water points.
Structural measures include adjusted working hours.

A cold wave is a significant drop in minimum temperature below the normal climatological average during the winter season.
The main cold-wave season in India is November to March.
The peak impact of cold waves in India occurs during December to February.
The India Meteorological Department is the nodal agency for forecasting cold waves.
The NDMA Guidelines on Cold Wave and Frost were issued in 2021.
A cold wave is a notified disaster eligible for assistance under the SDRF and NDRF.
The minimum-temperature threshold for declaring a cold wave in plains is 10°C or below.
In plains, a cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure of 4.5°C to 6.4°C.
In plains, a severe cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure greater than 6.4°C.
For plains based on actual temperature, a cold wave is declared when the actual minimum temperature is 4°C or below.
For plains based on actual temperature, a severe cold wave is declared when the actual minimum temperature is 2°C or below.
The minimum-temperature threshold for declaring a cold wave in hilly regions is 0°C or below.
In hilly regions, a cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure of 4.5°C to 6.4°C.
In hilly regions, a severe cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure greater than 6.4°C.
The minimum-temperature threshold for declaring a cold wave at coastal stations is 15°C or below.
At coastal stations, a cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure of 4.5°C or more.
A cold day is declared when the maximum temperature departure is –4.5°C to –6.4°C while the minimum temperature is already low.
A severe cold day is declared when the maximum temperature departure is less than –6.4°C.
Cold waves can cause respiratory diseases.
Cold waves can increase mortality among elderly people and children.
Homeless people are among the groups most vulnerable to cold waves.
Elderly people are among the groups most vulnerable to cold waves.
Children are among the groups most vulnerable to cold waves.
Outdoor workers are among the groups most vulnerable to cold waves.
Street vendors are among the groups most vulnerable to cold waves.
Poor households are among the groups most vulnerable to cold waves.
Cold waves affect agriculture through crop damage due to frost.
The IMD issues colour-coded cold-wave alerts.
The IMD cold-wave alert colours are Yellow, Orange and Red.
The NDMA guidelines focus on preparedness.
The NDMA guidelines focus on vulnerability mapping.
The NDMA guidelines focus on community awareness.
Protective measures against cold waves include distributing warm clothing.
Protective measures against cold waves include providing night shelters.
Protective measures against cold waves include establishing community kitchens.
Protective measures against cold waves include medical preparedness.
Agricultural measures against cold waves include frost-protection techniques for crops.

WCDRR stands for World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction.
The United Nations organised the WCDRR.
The purpose of WCDRR conferences is to discuss and adopt international frameworks for disaster risk reduction.
Three WCDRR conferences have been held.
All three WCDRR conferences were hosted by Japan.
UNDRR was the coordinating body for the 2nd and 3rd WCDRR conferences.
UNDRR was formerly known as UNISDR.
The 1st WCDRR was held in Yokohama, Japan.
The outcome document of the 1st WCDRR was the Yokohama World Strategy and Plan of Action for a Safer World.
The 2nd WCDRR was held in Kobe, Japan (Hyogo).
The outcome document of the 2nd WCDRR was the Hyogo Framework for Action (HFA) 2005–2015.
The 3rd WCDRR was held in Sendai, Japan.
The outcome document of the 3rd WCDRR was the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030.
The Yokohama Strategy was adopted in 1994.
The period of the Yokohama Strategy was from 1994 onwards.
The Yokohama Strategy provided the first global guidelines on disaster prevention, preparedness and mitigation.
The Hyogo Framework for Action was adopted in 2005.
The period of the Hyogo Framework for Action was 2005–2015.
The Hyogo Framework for Action focused on building the resilience of nations and communities.
The Hyogo Framework for Action had five priorities for action.
The Sendai Framework was adopted in 2015.
The period of the Sendai Framework was 2015–2030.
The Sendai Framework is the current global framework.
The Sendai Framework has four priorities.
The Sendai Framework has seven global targets.
The Sendai Framework includes the “Build Back Better” concept.
